text: Jesus left the temple and was walking away when his disciples came up to point out to him the temple buildings.
But he answered them, "Do you see all this? I tell you the truth: not one stone here will be left on another; every one will be torn down."
As he sat on the Mount of Olives, the disciples came to him privately and said, "Tell us, when will this happen, and what will be the sign of your coming and of the end of the age?"
Jesus answered them, "See to it that no one leads you astray.
For many will come in my name, saying, 'I am the Christ,' and they will lead many astray.
You will hear of wars and rumors of wars, but see that you are not alarmed. This must happen, but the end is not yet.
For nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom, and there will be famines and earthquakes in various places.

versions.text: Nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom, and there will be famines and earthquakes in various places.
versions.explanation: The connective γάρ links this verse as the explanation of verse 6 ("the end is not yet"). Restoring "For" preserves the flow of the discourse without harming the oral rhythm.

text: All these are only the beginning of the birth pains.
"Then they will hand you over to be persecuted and put to death, and you will be hated by all nations because of my name.
Then many will fall away, and they will betray one another and hate one another.
Many false prophets will arise and lead many astray.
And because lawlessness will increase, the love of most people will grow cold.
But the one who endures to the end will be saved.
And this gospel of the kingdom will be proclaimed throughout the whole world as a testimony to all nations, and then the end will come.
"So when you see the abomination of desolation, spoken of by the prophet Daniel, standing in the holy place—let the reader understand—
then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains.
Whoever is on the roof must not go down to get anything out of the house,
and whoever is in the field must not turn back to get his cloak.
How terrible it will be in those days for women who are pregnant or nursing!
Pray that your flight will not be in winter or on a Sabbath.
For then there will be great distress, such as has not happened from the beginning of the world until now, and never will again.
If those days had not been cut short, no one would survive; but for the sake of the elect they will be cut short.
"At that time, if anyone says to you, 'Look, here is the Christ!' or, 'There he is!'—do not believe it.
For false christs and false prophets will arise and perform great signs and wonders, so as to lead astray, if possible, even the elect.
See, I have told you beforehand.
So if they say to you, 'Look, he is in the wilderness,' do not go out; or, 'Look, he is in the inner rooms,' do not believe it.
For as the lightning comes from the east and flashes as far as the west, so will be the coming of the Son of Man.
Wherever the corpse is, there the vultures will gather.
"Immediately after the distress of those days the sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light; the stars will fall from the sky, and the powers of the heavens will be shaken.
Then the sign of the Son of Man will appear in the sky, and then all the tribes of the earth will mourn, and they will see the Son of Man coming on the clouds of heaven with power and great glory.

versions.text: Then the sign of the Son of Man will appear in the sky, and all the tribes of the earth will mourn as they see the Son of Man coming on the clouds of heaven with power and great glory.
versions.explanation: The Greek has two coordinated future verbs (κόψονται ... καὶ ὄψονται): they will mourn, and they will see. Rendering the second as a subordinate clause ("as they see") reverses the logical order and subordinates a main statement. Keeping both as parallel clauses is more accurate and reads well aloud.

versions.text: Then the sign of the Son of Man will appear in the sky, and all the tribes of the earth will mourn, and they will see the Son of Man coming on the clouds of heaven with power and great glory.
versions.explanation: The Greek repeats τότε ("and then") before the mourning clause, marking a second stage in the sequence. Restoring the second "then" preserves the emphatic repetition of the source and gives the sentence a clearer forward movement when read aloud, without disturbing the two parallel main verbs established in the earlier revision.

text: And he will send out his angels with a loud trumpet call, and they will gather his elect from the four winds, from one end of the heavens to the other.
"Learn this lesson from the fig tree: as soon as its branch grows tender and puts out leaves, you know that summer is near.

versions.text: "Learn this lesson from the fig tree: as soon as its branches grow tender and put out leaves, you know that summer is near.
versions.explanation: The Greek subject is singular (ὁ κλάδος, "its branch"). The singular also keeps the image concrete and the rhythm crisp for oral reading.

text: So also, when you see all these things, you know that he is near, right at the door.
I tell you the truth: this generation will certainly not pass away until all these things have happened.
Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will never pass away.
"But about that day and hour no one knows—not even the angels of heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father.
As it was in the days of Noah, so will be the coming of the Son of Man.
For in the days before the flood, people were eating and drinking, marrying and being given in marriage, right up to the day Noah entered the ark;
and they knew nothing about it until the flood came and swept them all away. So will it be at the coming of the Son of Man.
Then two men will be in the field; one will be taken and the other left.
Two women will be grinding at the mill; one will be taken and the other left.
So stay awake, because you do not know on what day your Lord is coming.
But understand this: if the owner of the house had known at what time of night the thief was coming, he would have kept watch and would not have let his house be broken into.
So you too must be ready, because the Son of Man will come at an hour you do not expect.
"Who then is the faithful and wise servant, whom the master has put in charge of his household to give the others their food at the proper time?
Blessed is that servant whom the master finds doing so when he returns.
I tell you the truth, he will put him in charge of all his possessions.
But suppose that wicked servant says to himself, 'My master is staying away a long time,'
and he begins to beat his fellow servants and to eat and drink with drunkards.
The master of that servant will come on a day he does not expect and at an hour he does not know.
He will cut him to pieces and assign him a place with the hypocrites. There, there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.

versions.text: He will cut him to pieces and assign him a place with the hypocrites, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.
versions.explanation: In Greek the final clause stands as its own sentence introduced by ἐκεῖ ("there"), a solemn refrain repeated elsewhere in this Gospel. Making it a separate sentence rather than a relative clause preserves that emphatic, self-standing quality and gives the oral reader a stronger closing cadence. A footnote on "cut him to pieces" could also note that the verb διχοτομήσει describes a severe punishment for an unfaithful slave.
